Abstract
The biomass-derived carbon-based electrode materials have gained huge attention due to their cost-effective prepara -
tion. Therefore, this study proposed the derivation of hierarchical carbon nanosheets from rice husks via carbonization 
and activation in KOH at different temperatures (600, 700, 800, and 900 °C). The inactivated carbon material exhibits 
the lowest surface area of 69 m 2g− 1 and becomes the largest (1985 m 2g− 1) at an activation temperature of 900 °C. The 
increasing activation temperature enhances the structural ordering and partial stacking of graphene layers. The I D/IG ratio 
decreases from 0.94 to 0.24 with increasing the activation temperature from 600 to 900 °C, which reflects the etching 
of the amorphous carbon. At maximum activation temperature (900 °C), the carbon materials progressively exfoliated 
into few-layer graphene-based nanosheets, offering high surface area. The intensity ratios of sp 2/sp3 hybridized carbon is 
increased (2.95–9.14) with increasing temperature, thereby indicating increasing graphitization. The maximum specific 
capacitance of 914 Fg − 1 at a current density of 0.75 Ag − 1 is calculated for the sample activated at 900 °C. The sample 
activated at 900 °C is demonstrates cyclic stability of 96% after 10,000 cycles and charge transfer resistance of 0.062 
ohms. The assembled symmetric supercapacitive device displays a specific capacitance of 214 F/g at 0.5 A/g, capacitance 
retention of 95.23% for 10,000 cycles, and minimum power of 532 W/kg at maximum energy density of 29 Wh/kg.

1 Introduction
The environmental contamination is growing due to the 
continuous consumption of non-renewable fossil fuels to 
overcome the severe energy crisis in recent decades. There-
fore, it is highly required to replace consumption of fossil 
fuel with the utilization of renewable natural resources. 
The biomass materials are ideal candidates for energy con -
version and energy storage applications due to their high 
surface area (SA), porosity, facile availability, and rich 
heteroatoms, including O, S, N, and P [ 1–4]. However, 
the natural degradation and combustion of biomass mate -
rials also produce environmental pollution. Therefore, it 
is highly recommended to utilize biomass materials waste 
(BMW) for fabrication of electrode materials of energy stor-
age devices in order to control their natural degradation and 
environmental pollution. The BMW can be used effectively 
to produce electrode materials for portable energy storage 
devices like supercapacitors (SCs), rechargeable batteries, 
owing to their unique SA and porosity [ 5–7]. Among these 
energy storage devices, the SC are remarkable due to high 
power density (P d), excellent cyclic life, and environmen -
tally safe operation. The satisfactory electrical conductivity, 
larger SA, and hierarchical pore distributions are promis -
ing in BMW-derived electrode materials, enabling them 
for electrical double-layer capacitive (EDLCs) behavior 
[8–11]. However, the OH− or H+ ions in the electrolyte can 
react with existing heteroatoms during Faradic redox reac -
tion and hence show pseudocapacitive behavior. Different 
BMW, including rice husk [ 12], walnut shell [ 13], date 
seeds [14], flowers [15], and abutilon theophrasti [16], were 
utilized to prepare electrode materials. However, a large 
enhancement in specific capacitance (C p) and energy den -
sity (Ed) is needed to meet the wider practical applications.

The BMW-derived electrode materials show a promising Cp 
contributed from EDLCs behavior. Therefore, overall elec -
trochemical performance can be boosted effectively by the 
introduction of pseudocapacitive behavior in BMW derived 
electrode materials [17–19].
The BMW-derived activated carbon (AC) is used in gas 
capturing, power storage and catalyst carriers [ 20, 21]. The 
adsorption of electrolyte ions is maximum on the large spe-
cific SA of AC electrode materials [22]. The unique physical 
and chemical properties of AC make it a promising material 
for different applications. The carbon-based materials are 
identified with large SA, pore volume, and different active 
sites for possible addition/diffusion of different atoms, which 
can take part in different chemical functions. The hydrogen, 
oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus, and halogen atoms 
can be inserted to tune the functionalities of carbonaceous 
materials [22, 23]. The heteroatoms increase the adsorption, 
gas separation, and selectivity properties of carbon materi -
als [24]. However, the adsorption processes are influenced 
by SA and porosity in addition to the presence of hetero -
atoms in the AC lattice [ 25]. Previous studies concluded 
that mostly BMW based materials show large microporous 
and ultra-microporous volumes with mesoporous and mac -
roporous structures [ 26]. These unique physical properties 
enable carbon materials for water filtration, separation of 
gas mixtures, catalysis, and energy storage devices [27–29].
Different physical and chemical treatments are applied 
to BMW to degrade their initial structure and convert 
them into AC materials [ 30, 31]. The activation process 
parameters and type of starting source materials generally 
decide the properties of derived AC materials. For example, 
pitch, peat, and coal were chemically treated to get coals 
for industrial applications [ 32–34]. BMW, including wood 
waste, plant materials, and food industry waste, can be bet -
ter alternatives to non-renewable sources [35]. Amid differ-
ent BMW, rice husks are highly attractive due to their large 
CO2 absorption, fast preparation rate, ability for water and 
soil filtration, and cultivation process requires low water, 
fertilizers, and pesticides [ 36, 37]. Different physical and 
chemical methods are primarily introduced to activate and 
produce AC from rice husks biomass [ 38]. The materials 
with high carbon contents can be formed by removing vola-
tile fractions and water from biomass by using an activation 
method. A high temperature range from 800 to 1100 °C is 
required in the physical method [ 39]. The biomass activa -
tion phase is related to heating rate and activation tempera -
ture [40]. The activation process should be done in an inert 
gas atmosphere with a reducing agent to promote dehy -
dration and graphitization reactions. All these processes 
increase the surface properties with different functionaliza -
tion [40]. The different gases, including Ar, N 2, H2O, CO, 
and He, are commonly used during the physical activation 
process of biomass materials. The surface properties are 
altered by enhancing the oxygen-containing surface func -
tional groups which can be increased by using water during 
physical activations. These oxygen-containing functional 
groups can be further included by using water and tempera-
ture control during hydrothermal physical activation meth -
ods [ 41]. During the hydrothermal process, the insertion 
of oxygen-containing functional groups at the surface can 
be promoted by using agents in a temperature range from 
150 to 300 °C. The carbonaceous materials generated by 
the physical activation method show a small pore volume as 
compared to the porous volume generated by the chemical 
activation method.
The chemical activation methods used both acidic 
(H2SO4, CH 3COOH, H 3PO4) and basic (NaOH, KOH, 
K2CO3) activating agents to increase the porosity of the car-
bon materials [42–45]. Among all activators, KOH is better 
suited to develop AC or graphene from biomass sources in 
oxygen oxygen-free environment. The KOH-activated AC 
shows high SA, porosity, and volume with different mor -
phologies. The gasification reaction can be promoted by 
releasing metal ions or by the addition of different func -
tional groups by using different salts as activating agents, 
like ZnCl2, FeCl3, KCl, NH 3, H2O, and urea [ 46–48]. The 
optimal treatment conditions can be regulated to get good 
porous AC by using single-step or two-step activation meth-
ods. For example, N. Dhashnamoorthy et al. used a chemi -
cal activation method to synthesize AC from Palmyra palm 
tree [49]. The AC electrode yielded a SA of 4600 m 2g− 1, 
a Cp of 553 Fg − 1 at 1 Ag− 1, and a cyclic stability of 165% 
after 10,000 cycles. The symmetric supercapacitor device 
also revealed a Cp of 164 Fg− 1 at 1 Ag− 1. K. Vengadesan et 
al. derived biocarbon from Palmyra palm seeds using 0.5 
M H2SO4, which exhibited a C p of 276 Fg − 1 at 1 Ag− 1 and 
63% capacitance retention after 500 cycles [ 50]. A.R. Sal-
varaj et al. derived AC nanosheets out of the evilest wood. 
The AC nanosheets presented a specific SA of 2943 m2g− 1, 
Cp of 588 Fg − 1 at 0.5 Ag − 1 and 92% cyclic retention after 
6000 cycles [ 51]. The symmetric supercapacitive device 
demonstrated Cp of 426 Fg − 1, Ed of 32 Whkg − 1, and P d of 
56 Wkg− 1. S.R. Mangisetti et al. developed N-S co-doped 
graphene nanosheets derived from biomass tender palm 
shoots [ 52]. The biomass-derived electrode demonstrated 
Cp of 529 Fg− 1 at 1.5 Ag− 1, and Ed of 106 Whkg− 1 and 93% 
cyclic retention after 10,000 cycles. It is observed that the 
preparation of graphene nanosheets from rice husks as pre -
cursors is not well reported and is still a major challenge. 
The present available methods of preparation are not good 
due to their high cost, complex process and incompatible to 
the surrounding. The AC nanostructures prepared by cur -
rent methods do not show well developed porous structure 
and high degree of graphitization that resulting in lower

electrochemical performance. The earlier reported works 
primarily focus on choice of precursor and activator. How -
ever, according to our knowledge little attentions were paid 
in term of temperature optimization to get high porosity and 
graphitization of AC by controlling the porous framework 
of BMW matrices. In this work, a systematic approach is 
proposed to derive AC from rice husks, a sustainable and 
low utilization BMW. The AC materials were prepared via 
carbonization process following by KOH activation at dif -
ferent controlled temperatures (600–900 °C). The chemical 
and structural properties were distinct by varying the acti -
vation temperature, showing the major role of temperature 
in converting BMW into a promising AC material. In this 
research work, the strong acidic activators are not used as 
compared to other AC preparation processes, which makes 
it simpler by just controlling the activation temperature. The 
RH-900 has high C p, cyclic stability, and chemical stabil -
ity making it useful for the fabrication of high-performance 
supercapacitors, as well as a viable process for BMW to 
produce AC electrode material. The Cp of 489, 651, 783 and 
914 Fg− 1 at 0.75 Ag− 1 is calculated for samples activated at 
600, 700, 800, and 900 °C.
2 Experimental
2.1 Materials and Reagents
The rice husks biomass carbon was obtained from Jhang vil-
lage, Pakistan. The biomass carbon source was sliced into 
small pieces, which were washed multiple times with deion-
ized water and then an oven at 80 °C for 24 h. The obtained 
carbon source was activated in KOH, while HCl and HF 
were applied to maintain its neutrality.
2.2 Preparation of Samples
The rice husks were washed with deionized water, dried at 
60 °C for 24 h and grind into a fine powder. The fine powder 
was passed through a 100-mesh sieve to get a homogeneous 
concentration of the nanoparticles in the powder. This pre -
cursor was carbonized under a continuous nitrogen gas flow, 
heated at 400 ℃ at a rate of 5 ℃ min −¹ and maintained at 
this temperature for 3 h to get biomass char (Fig. 1).
The biomass was gently mixed with KOH at a precise 
mass ratio of 1:3 in deionized water and stirred for 6 h to 
ensure uniform dispersion. Afterwards, the prepared slurry 
was dried in a vacuum furnace at 80 ℃ for 14 h. Then ground 
and exposed to thermal activation in a tube furnace under N₂ 
at 5 ℃ min − 1 to the target temperatures (600, 700, 800, or 
900 ℃), followed by a 3 h isothermal hold. The activated 
material were natural cooling and rinsed with deionized 
water to remove impurities and residual KOH. Moreover, 
inorganic impurities in the materials were eliminated by 
immersing them in HF (5 wt%) and HCl (10 wt%). The pre-
pared materials were dried in the vacuum oven at 80 °C for 
24 h to get the porous carbon. The obtained samples were 
named as RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and RH-900 elec-
trode materials.

2.4 Preparation of Electrode Materials
The working electrode was prepared by making a mixture 
of 5 mg of prepared material, 40 µL of Nafion solution, 400 
µL of deionized water, and 400 µL of pure ethanol. This 
mixture was sonicated for 6 h to get a slurry. The glassy 
carbon electrode was polished, and 3.2 µL of the slurry was 
deposited onto its surface and dried naturally. The electro -
chemical properties, including cyclic voltammetry (CV), 
galvanostatic charging-discharging (GCD), and electro -
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of the deposited 
RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and RH-900 electrode 
materials were analyzed by using three three-electrode elec-
trochemical workstation. The reference electrode of Hg/
HgO and counter electrode of platinum sheet were used 
to analyze the electrochemical performance of the work -
ing electrodes in 6 M KOH electrolyte. The CV profiles of 
each electrode were analyzed at different scan rates of 5, 
10, 30, 50, 70, 100, and 150 mVs − 1, whereas GCD profiles 
were analyzed at current densities of 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 
50 Ag− 1 in a potential range of 0 to -1.2 V . The symmetric 
supercapacitive device was assembled, and electrochemical 
performance was analyzed at different scan rates and cur -
rent densities in the same potential range. The Cp, Ed, and Pd

3 Results and Discussion
3.1 Surface Area
The N 2 adsorption-desorption isotherms were used to 
investigate the specific surface area (SA) and pore size 
distribution (PSD) of the RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, 
and RH-900 electrode materials. The inactivated electrode 
material is exhibited very low N 2 adsorption, as shown in 
Fig. 2A. The N 2 adsorption is increased after activation in 
KOH, as well as by increasing the activation temperature. 
The inactivated AC electrode is exhibited the lowest SA of 
69 m 2g− 1, which was increased with KOH activator. The 
increasing N2 adsorption in KOH-activated AC electrodes 
shows the growth of a porous structure with high SA. The 
type I features in the IUPAC classification and type H4 
hysteresis loops were exhibited by all electrodes, showing 
coexistence of microspores and mesoporous in the prepared 
RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and RH-900 electrode 
materials. The SA of RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and 
RH-900 electrode materials was 69, 1456, 1493, 1905 and 
1985 m2g− 1 as shown in Fig. 2B (Table 1).
The KOH activation and increasing activation tempera -
ture show significant effects in changing the SA of RH 
electrode material. The SA was increased with increasing 
activation temperature to 900 °C due to the coexistence of 
microspores with small mesopores at 900 °C. Figure 2C 
shows the PSDs of RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and 
RH-900 electrode materials. The PSD is concentrated at 
1–12 nm, confirming the existence of microspores and mes-
opores in the said electrodes. The average PSD of1.90, 2.10, 
2.19, 3.68 and 4.94 nm with pore volume of 0.086, 0.766, 
0.921, 1 and 1.376 cm3 for RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, 
and RH-900 electrode materials (Fig. 2D) [Table 1]. The 
RH-900 electrode material was exhibited a larger PSD of 
4.94 nm and pore volume of 0.086 cm3 g− 1. The micropores 
were widened into mesopores as the activation temperature 
is increased, resulting in larger pore volume in addition to 
reducing SA. The intensified KOH-induced etching and 
progressive pore development have increased the adsorp -
tion capacity with increasing temperature from 600 to 
900 °C. It is concluded that RH-900 is exhibited maximum 
SA, which is beneficial for large C p, shows large pore vol -
ume and mesopore, enabling fast ion transportation. The SA 
of the RH-900 electrode is larger than other carbon-based 
electrodes [6, 12, 17, 49].
3.2 Structural Analysis
The X-ray diffractometer was used to analyze the crystal 
structure of RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and RH-900 
electrode materials. Figure 3A shows the XRD pattern of

carbon materials derived from rice husks activated in KOH 
at different temperatures 600 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C. 
Two diffraction peaks, including (002) and (100) planes, 
were displayed at 25.6 o and 43.87 o related to turbostratic 
carbon [11, 57, 58]. The (002) plane is broad, whereas the 
(100) plane is sharper, as the broad peak shows the presence 
of a layer of graphene. This plane also shows the partially 
ordered graphitic domains instead of completely crystallized 
graphite [59, 60]. The peak intensity of (002) becomes high, 
showing enhanced structural ordering and partial stacking 
of graphene layers as the activation temperature is increased 
from 600 to 900 °C. It is concluded that the rising activation 
temperature promotes the rearrangement of carbon atoms 
into well-oriented graphitic structures.
Figure 3B shows the Raman spectra of the RH sam -
ples activated at different temperatures, including 600 °C, 
700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C. The carbon-based materials 
is highlighted the characteristic bands like D, G, and 2D. 
The D band at ~ 1352 cm− 1 represents structural defects and 
disordered carbon, and the G band at ~ 1590 cm− 1 displays 
in-plane vibrations of sp2-bonded carbon atoms in graphitic 
domains. The 2D band at ~ 2695 cm− 1 corresponds to stack-
ing and graphene layers in the said electrodes [ 61, 62]. The 
increasing activation temperature has changed the order -
ing of graphitic carbon, as indicated by the weakening of 
the D band and the intensity of the G band. The increasing 
temperature has changed the stacking of graphene layers, 
as validated by the presence of a 2D band. These variations 
in Raman bands enabled the transition of defective carbon 
into highly ordered graphene-like materials at the highest 
temperature.
The contributions from individual Raman modes can be 
studied separately by deconvolution of the Raman spec -
trum for each electrode. Figure 3C shows the deconvo -
luted Raman spectrum with I, D, D″, G, and D′ bands. At 
low activation temperature (600, 700 °C), I, D, D′, and D″ 
bands are stronger, indicating high structural defects, poor 
crystalline carbon, and larger disorder in the carbon lattice 
[63, 64]. The high defect density was also confirmed by the

3.3 Surface Morphology

analysis was used to depict the progressive transition in

als activated at different temperature (600, 700, 800, and 
900 °C). Figure 4 shows the transformation in surface mor-
phology of carbon-based materials with different activa -
tion temperatures. At 600 °C, the RH-600 sample shows 
relatively dense and compact structures with few cracks 
and limited porosity (Fig. 4A). These cracks are supporting

At 700 °C, the lamellar flakes are emerging, showing the

where intercalation of metallic potassium and gasification 
reactions expand the carbon lattice and create a hierarchical 
pore network, critical for high-performance EDLC (electric 
double-layer capacitor) behavior.
3.4 XPS Analysis
The distribution of different elements and bonding states 
in RH, RH-600, RH-700, RH-800, and RH-900 electrode 
materials is analyzed by XPS measurements. Figure 5 
demonstrates the XPS results for in RH, RH-600, RH-700, 
RH-800, and RH-900 electrode materials. The XPS survey 
was revealed the development of two significant peaks, C 1s 
and O 1s at binding energies of 283.8 and 532.3 eV , respec-
tively (Fig. 5A). Whereas, a weakly intense N 1s peak was 
also developed at a binding energy of 400.2 eV [ 46, 47]. 
The development of these three peaks at specific binding 
energies in the XPS survey spectrum validates the growth of 
carbon-based materials at different activation temperatures. 
The C, O, and N contents in the RH electrode material are 
82.43%, 16% and 1.57% respectively. However, these con-
tents at minimum activation temperature are 89.24%, 9.77% 
and 0.99%, whereas at maximum activation temperature 
are 94.46%, 4.78% and 0.76% respectively (Fig. 5B). The 
increasing temperature has altered the C, O, and N contents, 
as C contents are increased, whereas O and N contents were 
decreased (Fig. 5B). It was also revealed by the XPS sur -
vey that the C 1s peak becomes more intense in contrast to 
the O 1s peak with increasing activation temperature. The 
variations in peak intensities also revealed the increasing C 
contents but decreasing O contents with increasing activa -
tion temperatures. The C contents are increased due to the 
boosting of the etching process by the KOH activator, as 
O and N functional groups are exacerbated by the reaction 
activator [69, 70].

The high-resolution spectrum of C 1s exhibited four 
peaks at 283.8, 284.78, 288.49, and 291.51 in RH, RH-600, 
RH-700, RH-800, and RH-900 electrode materials (Fig. 5C–
G). The presence of these peaks is associated with C = O, 
shake-up satellite peak π → π * (sp 2 conjugated carbon 
peak), and sp 3 hetero conjugated carbon peak accordingly. 
It is observed that these carbon materials are formed due 
development of multiple conjugated systems, which is vali-
dated by π → π * peaks. The sp 2 hybridized carbon peaks 
become intense and narrower with rising activation tem -
perature [71–73]. The intensity ratios of sp 2/sp3 hybridized 
carbon are increased (2.95–9.14) with increasing tempera -
ture, thereby indicating increasing graphitization (Fig. 5H). 
These XPS results are according to Raman results and con-
firm the successful preparation of porous graphene using 
reversible rice husks as a carbon source.
The high-resolution O 1s spectrum is also plotted to study 
the presence of carbonyl (C = O), phenol/ether group (C-O), 
and carboxylic acid/chemically adsorbed oxygen/water 
(COOH/O2/H2O) groups (Inset image Fig. 5C-G). These 
groups are confirmed by their peaks at 530.72, 532.12, 
and 536.23 eV , respectively. The RH electrode exhibits 
42.09%, 52.21% and 5.71% of C = O, C-O, and COOH/O2/
H2O groups (Fig. 5I). The C = O contents are decreased in 
the presence of KOH activator. Whereas, C = O contents 
are increased with increasing the activation temperature. 
The C-O contents are decreased with increasing tempera -
tures. This illustrates that the highly unstable C-O groups 
developed at low temperature, which are decreased with 
increasing temperature. The domination of oxidative etch -
ing of carbon matrix by KOH activator has increased the 
C-O contents [ 74, 75]. The increasing activation tempera -
ture enhances the graphitization with porous nanosheets. 
The graphene nanosheets are formed by a complex crystal -
lization process of active sites assisted by potassium metal 
atoms. The different gases like CO, CO 2, etc., are released 
during the crystallization process that resulting in a lower 
content of C-O in the electrode, which is effective for maxi-
mum structure stability [76, 77].

The basic mechanism for KOH activation of biochar into 
graphitic carbon can be explained as the final carbon struc -
ture is strongly determined by the fact that KOH activation 
proceeds through a series of temperature-dependent redox, 
intercalation and gasification reactions. At lower activation 
temperatures (600, 700 °C), KOH reacts with amorphous 
carbons domains and unstable oxygen groups, resulting in 
some selective etching by releasing gaseous species like CO 
and CO2. The release of these gases produces initial micro-
pores. At high temperatures (800 and 900 °C), the KOH 
decomposition is more distinct, generating potassium and 
its intermediates which can intercalate between turbostratic 
carbon layers. This interlayer expansion fades van der 
Waals interactions and enhances the separation of stacked 
layers into graphene nanosheets. Moreover, the continuous 
etching widen the micropores into micro-mesoporous chan-
nels and developing a hierarchical porous graphitic carbon 
framework. The XPS results support this mechanism, where 
the progressive increase in sp²/sp³ ratio indicates conversion 
of disordered sp³-rich amorphous carbon into ordered sp² 
graphitic domains, while the reduction in oxygen content 
confirms decomposition of unstable surface functionalities 
during activation. These structural and chemical changes 
improve electrical conductivity, lower charge-transfer 
resistance, and enhance ion-accessible surface area, thereby 
contributing to the superior capacitive performance of 
RH-900.

4 Conclusions
In this study, hierarchical carbon nanosheets were derived 
from rice husks via carbonization and activation in KOH 
at different temperatures (600, 700, 800, and 900 °C). The 
inactivated material exhibited the lowest surface area of 69 
m2g− 1 and became the largest (1935 m2g− 1) at an activation 
temperature of 900 °C. The ID/IG ratio was decreased from 
0.94 to 0.24 with increasing the activation temperature from 
600 to 900 °C which reflected the etching of the amorphous 
carbon. The maximum C p of 914 Fg − 1 at a current density 
of 0.75 Ag− 1 is calculated for the RH-900 electrode mate -
rials. The RH-900 electrode material demonstrated cyclic 
stability of 96% after 10,000 cycles and R ct of 0.062 ohm. 
The assembled symmetric supercapacitive device displayed 
Cp of 214 F/g at 0.5 A/g, capacity retention of 95.23% for 
10,000 cycles, and minimum P d of 532 W/kg at maximum 
Ed of 29 Wh/kg.
